085c70f234817f6e: ISTANBUL: Deloitte Cyprus membantu oligarki Rusia, Roman Abramovich menyembunyikan sekurang-kurangnya USD10 bilion dalam bentuk aset dan didakwa mengelak cukai berjuta-juta dolar melalui dokumen dipalsukan, menurut satu siasatan yang diterbitkan pada Isnin, lapor Anadolu Ajansi.

Siasatan bersama oleh BBC, The Bureau of Investigative Journalism, The Guardian dan Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project membongkar lebih 1,000 rekod diundurkan tarikhnya membabitkan lebih 100 syarikat antara 1999 hingga 2013, termasuk dokumen digunakan untuk menyokong penyata kewangan mengelirukan.

Dalam satu kes, dokumen ditukar tarikh itu menyebabkan aset lebih USD10 bilion yang dipegang Electus Investments berpangkalan di Cyprus kelihatan seperti dimiliki sebuah syarikat dengan nama sama di British Virgin Islands, sekali gus membolehkan pegangan itu terlepas daripada keperluan pendedahan awam.

Dalam kes lain, akaun kewangan yang diluluskan Deloitte tidak memasukkan hartanah mewah, kapal persiaran mewah dan jet peribadi bernilai USD672 juta milik syarikat Abramovich, Amiscan Investments, menurut siasatan itu.

Penyiasat turut membongkar skim didakwa elak cukai membabitkan kira-kira USD2 bilion yang dipegang Kravin Investments. Dokumen diundurkan tarikh itu menyebabkan dana berkenaan kelihatan seperti milik syarikat luar pesisir lain, yang berpotensi membolehkan Kravin Investments mengelak cukai berjuta-juta dolar ke atas pendapatan faedah.

Peguam Abramovich menafikan beliau menyembunyikan aset, mengelak cukai atau secara sedar mengambil bahagian dalam pemalsuan tarikh itu, sambil menegaskan beliau bergantung secara sah kepada penasihat profesional.
Deloitte Cyprus memaklumkan ia "bertindak mengikut undang-undang berkuat kuasa" dan tidak dapat mengulas surat-menyurat khusus bertarikh lebih 20 tahun lalu.
Siasatan itu tidak menemui bukti pembabitan entiti Deloitte di luar Cyprus.
Abramovich, bekas pemilik Kelab Bola Sepak Chelsea, dikenakan sekatan oleh United Kingdom susulan perang di Ukraine pada 2022 atas dakwaan hubungannya dengan Presiden Vladimir Putin.
f92a19a0584e177f: SYDNEY: A Melbourne imam whose Islamic community centre has been linked by prosecutors in the United Arab Emirates to the co-pilot who allegedly attacked the captain of a flydubai jet has said he "never met" the man and insisted he has "consistently preached peace."

The Omani co-pilot, now in custody in the UAE, had drawn inspiration from Sept 11, 2001 suicide attacks, and carried out his attempt "with the aim of causing the greatest possible loss of life", according to the Emirati prosecutor's findings published by state media last week.

The prosecutor said the co-pilot first became radicalised while studying in Australia "through reading extremist literature and following online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks."
The prosecutor alleged he was acquainted there with an organisation known as "My Centre" managed by a Lebanese man called Abu Hamza.
Neither "My Centre" nor Abu Hamza are accused of any criminal wrongdoing.
In a statement posted on social media late on Monday, Abu Hamza – also named by local media as Samir Mohtadi – said he had "never met" the co-pilot identified in reports as Hamam al-Hammami.
"We have no record of him ever attending our centre," he said.
"The relevant authorities should have verified these claims with me before releasing or publishing such information," he added.
He said he had "consistently preached peace" throughout his life.
"We unequivocally reject violence in all its forms."
Police and intelligence services in Australia have said they are investigating the co-pilot's links to the country.
And police in New Zealand said last week he had spent time in the country on a six-month student visa, where he completed a portion of his flight training, national broadcaster RNZ said.--AFP
fc4a29e18095dedd: LONDON: Mikel Arteta said Piero Hincapie and Martin Zubimendi would both miss Arsenal's Champions League match with Lille after suffering freak ankle injuries in their warm-down after Saturday's win against Leeds.
Ecuador defender Piero Hincapie, a late substitute in the 2-1 victory at the Emirates, was carried off the pitch after hurting himself in the post-match session.

"We had a training session planned after the game for the players that didn't have enough minutes to get everybody the recovery day on Sunday, and to get everybody in the right rhythm, and in two very unfortunate actions, we lost two players, and yeah, not great," he said.
"We need to assess them. Today they have further scans to see where they are, and they will have a timeframe for how long they'll be out."
The Spaniard added: "What can you do? If I knew I had a crystal ball, I'd say, 'Guys, go in the jacuzzi, everybody, and see you tomorrow.'"
Arteta confirmed both players would miss the home game against French Ligue 1 team Lille on Tuesday, adding: "Piero's one looks a little bit more serious, I think, but we have to wait and see."
Last season's Champions League finalists beat Napoli in their opening match in the competition last month.
Arsenal are second in the Premier League, three points behind Manchester City.--AFP
d11deb8e88307308: SYDNEY: A Melbourne imam whose Islamic community centre has been linked by prosecutors in the United Arab Emirates to the co-pilot who allegedly attacked the captain of a flydubai jet has said he "never met" the man and insisted he has "consistently preached peace".

The Omani co-pilot, now in custody in the UAE, had drawn inspiration from Al-Qaeda's Sept 11, 2001 suicide attacks, and carried out his attempt "with the aim of causing the greatest possible loss of life", according to the Emirati prosecutor's findings published by state media last week.

The prosecutor said the co-pilot first became radicalised while studying in Australia "through reading extremist literature and following online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks".
The prosecutor alleged he was acquainted there with an organisation known as "My Centre" managed by a Lebanese man called Abu Hamza.
Neither "My Centre" nor Abu Hamza are accused of any criminal wrongdoing.
In a statement posted on social media late on Monday, Abu Hamza - also named by local media as Samir Mohtadi - said he had "never met" the co-pilot identified in reports as Hamam al-Hammami.
"We have no record of him ever attending our centre," he said.
"The relevant authorities should have verified these claims with me before releasing or publishing such information," he added.
He said he had "consistently preached peace" throughout his life.
"We unequivocally reject violence in all its forms."
Police and intelligence services in Australia have said they are investigating the co-pilot's links to the country.
And police in New Zealand said last week he had spent time in the country on a six-month student visa, where he completed a portion of his flight training, national broadcaster RNZ said.
d4e994a42990ef49: From Moaz Nair

The ghost of Malay politics past continues to haunt a fading Umno. Ever since its historic, humiliating downfall in the 2018 general election, the party has been trapped in a state of pathetic paralysis, desperately daydreaming about reclaiming its crown as the nation's undisputed political hegemon.

Yet, instead of executing a clear strategy, Umno's leadership is caught in a dilemma of cowardly choices: suck up to Pakatan Harapan in a volatile unity government, or venture into the wilderness alone, or crawl back to its treacherous former rival PAS.

This delusional "two-tier approach" – trying to play both sides by cutting different deals at the state and federal levels – is a weak political gimmick that has failed to fool anyone, least of all PAS.

Meanwhile, Umno’s relationship with PH has rapidly soured under its current leadership. By even flirting with PAS, a party that relentlessly trashes PH as secular and liberal, Umno is actively incinerating whatever fragile trust it has left with its current governing partners.
Let’s call a spade a spade: this is a desperate, toxic battle for survival.

After bloating itself on power for nearly six decades, Umno still blindly demands to be treated as the "Big Brother" of Malay politics. But wake up: PAS now holds the actual cards. Armed with a superior parliamentary seat count and total control over four state governments -- Kelantan, Terengganu, Kedah and Perlis -- PAS has effectively usurped the throne.
Walking into a trap

Analysts see right through Umno’s terror. The party knows that any formal alliance with the Islamic juggernaut will reduce Umno to the position of a weak, castrated junior partner. History has proven time and again that when these two egos clash over who commands Malay politics, a bloody political knife-fight is virtually guaranteed.
Besides, how short is Umno's memory?

The catastrophic collapse of the 2019 Muafakat Nasional pact should have been a permanent lesson. PAS didn't hesitate to stab Umno in the back, secretly conspiring with Bersatu to form Perikatan Nasional in 2020. Umno president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi openly branded that move a betrayal, and the party rank and file still rightly whisper that PAS carries a "DNA of betrayal".
To walk back into that trap is pure political suicide.

Any attempt at a reunion faces brutal realities: PAS will never surrender the safe, Malay-majority seats it currently locks down. It will greedily force Umno to run in highly volatile, hostile areas, guaranteeing an electoral wipeout of Umno's remaining footprint.

PAS’s aggressive youth wing and top leaders are no longer hiding their ambitions: they want a PAS prime minister. They will never yield the top job to a diminished Umno, shattering any illusion of an equal partnership.
Can Umno survive?

Umno’s traditional lifeline has always been its ability to bridge gaps using non-Malay votes. Crawling into bed with an uncompromising Islamist party will permanently alienate those voters, severing Umno's last remaining oxygen supply.

This desperate anxiety is already reeking at the state level. In Perak and Pahang, Umno leaders hold the posts of menteri besar only out of sheer charity by PH, not because Umno commands a real majority. Inviting PAS into these states is code for a hostile takeover. PAS will effortlessly leverage its momentum, hijack the state machinery, and relegate Umno to political irrelevance on its own turf.

PAS knows it doesn't need Umno; its most realistic path to absolute power remains firmly rooted in consolidating its Malay-Islamic framework. This leaves Umno stranded at a historic crossroads of its own making. Going solo in today’s fractured landscape offers zero guarantee of survival, yet leaping back into the arms of PAS ensures complete subordination to a green wave that has already captured the Malay-Muslim electorate.

If Umno wants to survive, it needs to snap out of its historical delusion. It can no longer demand the "Big Brother" crown based on past glory. It must adapt to a brutal new reality or get comfortable being buried in the footnotes of Malaysian history.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

491003425f09b13f: Lembaga politik Melayu silam nampaknya terus menghantui Umno yang kini kian malap.

Sejak kejatuhannya yang cukup memalukan dalam PRU14, parti itu terus terperangkap dalam kelumpuhan politik yang parah—sekadar dibuai mimpi untuk merampas semula mahkota sebagai hegemon politik negara yang mutlak.

Namun, alih-alih merangka strategi yang ampuh, kepimpinan Umno seolah-olah tersepit dalam dilema penakut: mahu terus menumpang teduh di bawah Pakatan Harapan (PH) dalam Kerajaan Perpaduan yang rapuh, merintis jalan sendiri secara solo, atau kembali menyorong sembah kepada bekas seteru ketatnya, PAS.

Pendekatan dua hala yang delusional ini—cuba bermain di kedua-dua belah pihak dengan mengintai ruang rundingan berbeza di peringkat negeri dan persekutuan—hanyalah gimik politik lemah yang gagal memperbodohkan sesiapa, terutamanya PAS.
Sementara itu, hubungan Umno dengan PH di bawah kepimpinan sedia ada kian hambar dan retak.

Tindakan Umno yang seakan memberi isyarat mesra kepada PAS—sebuah parti yang konsisten melabel PH sebagai sekular dan liberal—secara tidak langsung menghanguskan sisa-sisa kepercayaan rapuh yang masih ada bersama rakan gabungannya hari ini.
Kenyataan yang pahit harus ditelan: ini merupakan rona-rona perjuangan demi kelangsungan hidup yang penuh desperasi dan toksik.
Setelah hampir enam dekad dibuai kemewahan kuasa, Umno masih membuta tuli menuntut supaya dilayan sebagai 'abang besar' dalam politik Melayu.
Hakikatnya, Umno perlu berpijak di bumi nyata kerana PAS kini memegang carta politik sebenar.
Berbekalkan jumlah kerusi Parlimen yang lebih besar serta penguasaan mutlak di empat buah negeri (Kelantan, Terengganu, Kedah dan Perlis), PAS secara efektif telah merampas takhta kepimpinan itu.

Penganalisis politik melihat kecamuk ketakutan Umno ini dengan jelas. Parti itu sedar bahawa sebarang pakatan rasmi dengan gergasi Islamis tersebut hanya akan meletakkan Umno sebagai rakan junior yang mandul dan tidak bermaya.
Sejarah telah berulang kali membuktikan, apabila dua ego besar bertembung demi merebut pengaruh politik Melayu, pertembungan sengit yang menumpahkan darah politik pastinya tidak dapat dielakkan.
Lagipun, adakah memori Umno begitu singkat?
Kegagalan piagam Muafakat Nasional pada tahun 2019 sepatutnya menjadi iktibar yang kekal.
PAS sama sekali tidak teragak-agak untuk 'menikam' Umno dari belakang apabila secara rahsia bersekongkol dengan Bersatu demi melahirkan Perikatan Nasional (PN) pada tahun 2020.
Presiden Umno Zahid Hamidi sendiri secara terbuka melabelkan tindakan itu sebagai satu pengkhianatan, dan sehingga kini akar umbi parti masih berbisik bahawa PAS membawa 'DNA pengkhianatan'.
Justeru, kembali menyerah diri ke dalam perangkap yang sama adalah satu tindakan membunuh diri dalam politik.
Sebarang usaha ke arah penyatuan semula akan berdepan realiti yang amat getir.
PAS tidak akan sesekali menyerahkan kerusi selamat majoriti Melayu yang kini berada dalam genggaman mereka.
PAS sebaliknya akan mendesak Umno untuk bertanding di kawasan-kawasan berisiko tinggi dan bergolak, sekali gus menjamin pelupusan baki pengaruh pilihan raya Umno.
Malah, sayap Pemuda PAS dan pimpinan tertingginya kini tidak lagi berselindung tentang cita-cita mereka untuk melihat seorang perdana menteri daripada PAS.
Mereka tidak akan menyerahkan jawatan nombor satu negara itu kepada Umno yang kian mengecil, gusar memadam sebarang ilusi perkongsian kuasa yang setara.
Talian hayat tradisi Umno selama ini adalah keupayaannya untuk merapatkan jurang undi menerusi sokongan pengundi bukan Melayu.
Tindakan kembali ke ranjang bersama parti Islamis yang tegar ini hanya akan menjauhkan golongan pengundi itu buat selama-lamanya, sekali gus memutuskan talian oksigen terakhir Umno.
Kebimbangan yang mendesak ini sudah pun mula dihidu di peringkat negeri.
Di Perak dan Pahang, pemimpin Umno hanya mampu memegang jawatan menteri besar atas ihsan dan kebaikan PH—bukan kerana Umno menguasai majoriti sebenar.
Menjemput PAS ke negeri-negeri ini merupakan isyarat awal kepada pengambilalihan yang agresif.
PAS akan dengan mudah mempergunakan momentum sedia ada, merampas jentera negeri, dan akhirnya meminggirkan Umno sehingga menjadi tidak relevan di halaman sendiri.
PAS amat menyedari bahawa mereka tidak lagi memerlukan Umno; jalan paling realistik untuk meraih kuasa mutlak kekal berpaksi kepada pengukuhan kerangka Melayu-Islam mereka sendiri.
Situasi ini meninggalkan Umno terdampar di persimpangan jalan sejarah yang dibinanya sendiri.
Bergerak solo dalam landskap politik yang berpecah-belah hari ini tidak menjanjikan sebarang jaminan untuk kelangsungan hidup.
Namun, melompat kembali ke pangkuan PAS pula bermakna menyerah kalah secara total kepada gelombang hijau yang telah pun menawan minda sebahagian besar pengundi Melayu-Muslim.
Sekiranya Umno mahu terus bernafas, parti itu perlu segera bangkit daripada khayalan sejarahnya.
Ia tidak lagi boleh menuntut mahkota 'abang besar' bersandarkan kegemilangan masa lalu.
Umno wajib menyesuaikan diri dengan realiti baharu yang kejam ini, atau bersedia untuk terus terkubur dalam nota kaki sejarah Malaysia.

3254f22cfc4c4e5f: KUALA TERENGGANU: Long before concrete shoplots and modern commercial centres became the norm, rows of two-storey wooden shophouses formed the heart of trade in Kuala Dungun, Terengganu.
Known locally as "kedai kayu", many of these buildings date back to the 1930s and still stand today, their timber structures offering a glimpse into the town’s commercial past.

Trader and longtime resident Ang Ah Kiang, 76, said Kuala Dungun grew from a fishing settlement into an important trading centre, with economic activity expanding further alongside the rise of iron ore mining in nearby Bukit Besi.
The mining industry developed rapidly from the 1930s to the 1960s before the mine closed in 1970, bringing workers and business activity into the district.
“The economic growth also indirectly spurred trade in Kuala Dungun, including the emergence of various shops supplying the needs of residents and workers,” Ang told Bernama.
He said some of the wooden shophouses were built between 1930 and 1960, with about 100 units constructed during that period.
Many continue to serve the same basic purpose today, housing restaurants, hardware and electrical shops, motorcycle dealers, grocery stores, photo shops and other small businesses.
Among them is the restaurant operated by Kamal Hamid, 59, who has been renting one of the more-than-90-year-old premises since 1986. Prior to which, his father rented the same shop.
Although the building has undergone several renovations over the decades, Kamal said its original structure has largely been retained.
“I was told that the original owner was a former employee of the iron ore-mining company in Bukit Besi, and that the building was purchased in the 1930s,” he said.
The story of the shophouses is closely tied to the development of Kuala Dungun itself.

Wan Rosli Wan Ngah, honorary secretary of the Dungun chapter of the Malaysian Historical Society, said the Dungun district office reorganised the town in 1933, creating wooden shoplots to support growing trade.
More Chinese residents settled during that period, buying land and newly completed shophouses. Malay residents living in the area were relocated to Kampung Tanah Lot.
Wan Rosli said Hokkien migrants from southern China had begun arriving in the district as early as 1922, with many settling around the Sungai Dungun estuary.
They opened businesses selling groceries, seafood and rubber before becoming closely associated with the wooden shophouses after the town’s reorganisation.

Today, the businesses may be different and the buildings altered in places, but the surviving kedai kayu remain part of Kuala Dungun’s everyday streetscape - reminders of how trade helped shape the town nearly a century ago.

2a72e051d5f2d258: LONDON: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham met Manchester City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak at an investment summit several years ago when he was mayor of the city, the Greater Manchester Combined Authority said on Monday.

The announcement comes after Burnham said he would be "really concerned" if City's owners sold the club following the decision to find the 10-time English champions guilty of breaching the Premier League's financial rules.
Burnham, who was mayor of Greater Manchester from 2017 to June 2026, faced criticism for appearing to express support for City's hierarchy.
Downing Street subsequently had to backtrack, insisting no one was "above the rules."
But there were demands for clarification regarding Burnham's relationship with City's owners, who have driven significant investment in Manchester through partnerships with local authorities.
City are owned by Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG), controlled by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan, a member of the United Arab Emirates royal family.

A Greater Manchester Combined Authority spokesman said: "In October 2021 Andy Burnham, in his role as mayor of Greater Manchester, had a formal meeting with Khaldoon Al Mubarak at the UK Government's Global Investment Summit arranged by the Department for International Trade.

"In his capacity as mayor, he was a guest of Manchester City FC at home matches on a small number of occasions, including attending Vincent Kompany's testimonial match in September 2019, where he met the chairman informally in the stands. These have been declared in the usual way."
The statement added that during Burnham's time as mayor "representatives of Greater Manchester sporting clubs would routinely join business delegations as part of mayoral international visits.

"This included representatives from Manchester United travelling to Austin and Dublin, Lancashire Cricket Club joining a delegation to India, and Manchester City FC staff supporting visits to China and Japan."

City have been found guilty of breaking more than 100 Premier League financial regulations by arranging "sham" contracts to artificially inflate revenues and reduce costs in a nine-season between 2009 and 2018.
The Premier League leaders have appealed against the verdict, saying it contains "clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe."
City could be hit with a huge points deduction or even face expulsion from the Premier League if they lose the appeal.
But Louie French, the opposition Conservatives spokesman for sport, said the statement contained "precious little information about these meetings, what was discussed and what may have been agreed."
It was far "from the full transparency that football fans deserve. Burnham cannot hide behind the GMCA - he must take responsibility for this himself", French added.--AFP

419a8cda131df0b9: WASHINGTON: US House speaker Mike Johnson said he had reservations about a planned livestreamed execution in an interview broadcast by CBS News on Monday.
Nidal Hasan, 56, was sentenced to be executed by firing squad on Dec 3 at Fort Hood, Texas, where he shot and killed 13 people in 2009.

The decision to livestream the execution - which would be the first US military execution by firing squad since 1945 - has drawn widespread blowback, with the top congressional Republican adding his voice to the mix.

"The concern would be that you would create a video that would be a recruiting tool for future terrorists," Johnson told CBS News, adding: "We've got to think through the policy implications of all that."
The Republican lawmaker said he would not watch the execution if it were broadcast live in any case.
"There are colleagues who have concerns," he said.
US defence secretary Pete Hegseth defended the idea to livestream the execution, saying "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public."
President Donald Trump for his part has said that a final decision on whether the execution would be broadcast live or not remained to be made.
9fd13be2f0ec729b: KUALA LUMPUR: The health ministry will recommend absorbing contract dental and pharmacy officers into permanent positions for the consideration of the finance ministry and Cabinet.
Health minister Dzulkefly Ahmad said the proposal would be pursued within a reasonable timeframe, based on the approach previously used to address the issue of contract medical doctors.
"...the first step will be followed by other service schemes, namely dentists and pharmacists as well," he said when met after appearing as a guest on Bernama TV’s Ruang Bicara programme last night.
He said the recruitment of dental and pharmacy officers into permanent positions would utilise a new quota separate from the 9,000 permanent medical doctor positions announced in the 2027 budget.

The Malaysian Dental Association had urged the government and health ministry to consider permanent appointments for contract dental officers following the announcement of permanent appointments for medical doctors.

Commenting on reports regarding dental officers whose contracts had ended without being renewed, Dzulkefly said the health ministry would continue to pay attention to their welfare and work experience within the public healthcare system.

On a separate matter, Dzulkefly expressed hope that the finance ministry would consider a request for a seed allocation of approximately RM100 million to strengthen the management of non-communicable diseases (NCDs) at the primary healthcare level.
He said the allocation was crucial for enhancing the prevention, screening, diagnosis, treatment and the continuous control of chronic diseases such as diabetes and high blood pressure.

"Matters related to NCD management are a major component I am bringing into the reforms. In addition to PeKa B40, which received an allocation of RM80 million, managing NCDs from a healthcare perspective is essential to effectively address this chronic disease pandemic," he said.

He said benchmarking per capita expenditure for NCD management also took into account practices in countries like Singapore and Indonesia, as well as global trends prioritising primary healthcare services.
d293e54442d5369a: PETALING JAYA: A transport think tank said the government must heed passenger capacity following the decision to implement the elevated autonomous rapid transit system to overcome congestion in Johor Bahru.

MY Mobility Vision executive director Rahman Hussin said there is a need to understand how many people are expected to use the system, particularly during peak hours. There was also a need to understand whether the proposed vehicle capacity and service frequency can accommodate that demand, he said.

Rahman said that passenger capacity is among the three areas that deserve careful attention. Other matters are: long-term operating and maintenance costs; and the impact on existing road traffic, particularly during construction and around major junctions.

“The assessment should consider not only construction expenditure but also infrastructure maintenance, vehicle replacement, energy consumption and technology support over the system’s lifespan,” he told FMT.

The government announced on Friday that the elevated autonomous rapid transit system (e-ART) had been chosen to solve congestion in Johor Bahru, backed by temporary measures including increased bus and KTM Komuter services, and Grab Shuttles around key density zones.

Rahman said the government should also examine how the autonomous system will be integrated with existing facilities and the Johor Bahru-Singapore rapid transit link which begins operations in mid-February.

“International experience shows that successful urban transport systems are designed around passenger demand, network integration and operational performance, rather than technology alone,” Rahman said.

Separately, transport consultant Rosli Azad Khan said e-ART vehicles offer nearly 10 times the capacity of standard stage buses, making them far better suited to absorb peak-hour crowds than ordinary bus fleets.
He said the elevated system would complement the RTS Link as they can accommodate a high number of passengers in one stop within Bukit Chagar.
Rosli said dedicated elevated corridors or separated lanes at road level will allow the e-ART vehicles to operate at maximum speed without being delayed by general traffic congestion.
"To make it more effective, the system should be introduced prior to the opening of RTS so that its route networks are established earlier and become more familiar to the public transport users.”

96cd2a9f9379bb8b: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 13 — Online shoppers could see clearer accountability for e-commerce platforms and sellers under a new law.
Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim announced when tabling Budget 2027 that the government had agreed to introduce a new law to replace Malaysia’s Electronic Commerce Act 2006.
If passed by Parliament and brought into force, the proposed legislation would strengthen accountability among online platforms and sellers.

Alongside this move, the government is also examining legislative and enforcement measures to protect local micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) from unfair competition and ensure products bought by consumers are safe.

The move follows the government’s decision to repeal and replace the 2006 Act, which Domestic Trade and Cost of Living Minister Datuk Armizan Mohd Ali said did not comprehensively define the responsibilities of platforms, sellers and other participants in online transactions.
On September 19, Armizan said the ministry had approved the policy decision to replace the existing law with a more comprehensive framework.
What does the Electronic Commerce Act 2006 not adequately cover?

The Ministry of Domestic Trade and Cost of Living’s (KPDN) through their review of Malaysia’s e-commerce regulatory framework, published in October 2025 had identified gaps in platform accountability and the wider regulatory framework.
There are several areas that the 2006 Act does not adequately address.
Regulating e-commerce platforms directly
The Act does not provide a comprehensive framework governing how online marketplaces must operate or what regulatory obligations they must fulfil.
Clearly defining platform accountability
It does not comprehensively establish the responsibilities of platforms when sellers engage in misleading or potentially harmful practices.
Regulating sellers and their conduct
The Act does not comprehensively regulate online sellers and their businesses.
Addressing cross-border e-commerce
The existing framework does not adequately address regulatory and enforcement challenges posed by overseas sellers and platforms serving Malaysian consumers.
Platform oversight and enforcement
There is no comprehensive legal framework addressing oversight of platforms and ensuring accountability.
Keeping pace with the wider digital marketplace
The Act does not adequately define the roles and responsibilities of intermediaries involved in product visibility, advertising, transactions and access to consumers.
So, what could change for people who shop online?
The Electronic Commerce Act 2006 primarily provides legal recognition for electronic transactions.
A new law could give shoppers greater clarity over a marketplace’s responsibilities when a seller offers misleading products, fails to fulfil an order or engages in questionable practices.
Will platforms have to do more to ensure products are safe?
Product safety is one of the concerns highlighted by the government.
In his Budget 2027 speech, Anwar said the government was examining legislative and enforcement measures to ensure goods bought by consumers were safe.

The government has also raised concerns about foreign e-commerce companies operating in the Malaysian market without adequate oversight. The proposed law is intended to examine a broader framework for regulating platforms and sellers.
Will it become easier to identify a seller?
Identifying the actual seller can be difficult when consumers make purchases through large online marketplaces, particularly when businesses operate from overseas.

KPDN’s review of the e-commerce regulatory framework considered stronger seller identification and information-disclosure requirements, including measures to help establish the identity of businesses operating online.
Such measures could help consumers make more informed purchasing decisions and give authorities better information when investigating complaints.
What if the seller is based overseas?
Cross-border transactions can complicate enforcement when a seller has no registered business entity in Malaysia.

Consumers who receive defective products, do not receive their orders or have disputes over transactions may find it difficult to pursue the seller, particularly if the business operates in another country.
The government has identified the regulation of foreign e-commerce businesses as an area requiring attention.

Armizan has also highlighted regulatory gaps affecting foreign sellers and said the government was studying ways to strengthen platform accountability and the application of Malaysian laws to overseas entities.
Will it be easier to resolve disputes and obtain refunds?
KPDN’s findings identified dispute resolution and consumer redress as areas requiring improvement, including the possibility of a more integrated online dispute-resolution mechanism.

In February, Armizan told Parliament that the ministry was considering a more comprehensive online dispute-resolution platform that could handle the process from filing a complaint to adjudication or a decision.
Such a system could make it easier for consumers to submit complaints and pursue disputes digitally.
Will online marketplaces need a licence?
Licensing is another regulatory option being considered to strengthen oversight of e-commerce platforms.

On September 19, Armizan had in a Bernama report said the government was studying the possibility of introducing a licensing regime, particularly in view of overseas goods entering the market, consumer safety and the sustainability of local MSMEs.
The distinction matters because registration, licensing and other compliance requirements can impose different obligations on businesses.
What happens next?

In his Budget 2027 speech, Anwar announced that the proposed e-commerce Bill would likely be tabled at the next Parliament sitting in March to strengthen accountability among online platforms and sellers.

The Bill’s detailed provisions will determine how far the reforms go, including whether they introduce new obligations for platforms, strengthen oversight of foreign sellers or create additional avenues for consumer redress.

Until the replacement law takes effect, existing legislation — including the Consumer Protection Act 1999 and the Consumer Protection (Electronic Trade Transactions) Regulations 2024 — continues to apply where relevant.
dc58aa05b89d1cad: WELLINGTON, Oct 13 — A bank in New Zealand has found itself at the centre of an unlikely free speech row after an attempt to remove “explicit” memes about its sheep mascot from social media.
Kiwibank unveiled the mascot “Buck” this year in an ad campaign urging consumers to “bank Kiwi”.
But the cute sheep with green wool quickly drew some unwanted attention online, with viral posts on X alluding to Buck’s good looks — and uncharitable references to stereotypes about New Zealanders.

The state-owned bank responded by sending takedown requests, removing the image of Buck in the offending posts and leaving only the phrase: “this media has been disabled in response to a report by the copyright owner”.
Users responded by barraging the platform with dozens more in its place, and the original post has now garnered over four million views.
“what if we ALL say the kiwibank sheep is sexy. They can’t get us all,” one social media user said.
Commentators described it as a classic example of the so-called “Streisand effect” — in which an attempt to hide something draws even greater attention to it.
Kiwibank spokesman Ben Mabon said the company had been responding to “explicit and harmful content being shared using Buck’s image”.
“Our concern was a serious one, and we believed it was important to address it,” he said in a statement to AFP.
“We recognise that the response became part of a conversation. We felt doing nothing wasn’t the right thing to do because of the harmful content.”
In an open letter to Kiwibank, New Zealand’s Free Speech Union accused the company of censorship.
“Copyright protects creative work from being copied. It does not protect a brand from being laughed at, even by people who like it a bit too much,” the letter read.
“Using copyright to remove speech a company dislikes is censorship, even when the subject is a sheep.”
New Zealand has long been known for having more sheep than people, with a ratio of 4.5 sheep to every person as of 2025. — AFP
6a460261f3a62547: MUAR, Oct 13 — What began as research into Malaysia’s forest treasures has successfully led to the development of a commercially viable perfume product derived from Aquilaria malaccensis, the agarwood species.
The Innovation Centre in Agritechnology for Advanced Bioprocessing (ICA) at Universiti Teknologi Malaysia (UTM) Pagoh Campus has developed the product, known as “Fragrad.”
This initiative paves the way for the commercialisation of university research while enhancing the value of agarwood, a resource often dubbed as “forest gold.”
ICA UTM Pagoh campus research officer Dr Norliza Abdul Latiff said the idea to create an agarwood-based perfume emerged in 2023 after she was captivated by the wood’s aroma during her research.
She noted that the concept received the backing of ICA director Prof Dr Hesham Ali El-Enshasy and was subsequently developed through a UTM research grant, involving a team of 13 experts.
“We want this research not merely to end in the laboratory but to be translated into innovations with commercial value.
“After about a year of developing the formulation, in 2024 we successfully produced an agarwood-based perfume named Fragrad,” she told Bernama when met recently.
Norliza, who is also the lead researcher for the ICA UTM Agarwood Perfume Project, said the formulation process involved several stages to ensure the scent remained consistent and long-lasting.
Fragrad currently comes in four fragrance variations namely SheGrad, HeGrad, Teja, and Tuah, developed to cater to diverse consumer preferences. — Bernama pic
She noted that the product was developed as one of UTM’s “signature” products and has the potential to serve as an exclusive university souvenir.
Fragrad currently comes in four fragrance variations namely SheGrad, HeGrad, Teja, and Tuah, developed to cater to diverse consumer preferences.
“All the fragrances utilise agarwood essence sourced from local suppliers, and the production process takes between three weeks and two months, depending on the grade and formulation,” she said.
She said about 25 per cent agarwood essence is used in each formulation before it is blended with other fragrance components and ingredients.

According to her, the use of local raw materials helps establish a value chain linking university research with the industry, while also expanding the potential of agarwood as a high-value downstream product.
However, she noted that securing a supply of high-quality agarwood essence remains a major challenge, as the raw material is not easily obtained and requires advance ordering from suppliers.
She added that ICA UTM aims to introduce at least one new agarwood-based product annually, in line with efforts to bring research outcomes to the market.
Fragrad is currently marketed through UTMart at UTM Skudai Campus in Johor Bahru, as well as via several online sales platforms.
She said nearly 300 bottles of the perfume have been produced so far, and ICA UTM targets sales exceeding 600 bottles over the three-year commercialisation period from 2024 to 2027. — Bernama
d4cc7aabe8176b8f: For decades, South Asia was locked in a perpetual cycle of conflict management: brief military clashes between India and Pakistan would be followed by de-escalation and the resumption of formal peace talks, which eventually gave way to another bout of conflict. But this pattern has now been broken.

No high-level dialogue has taken place since 2016. Rather than some temporary diplomatic tantrum, this reflects a paradigm shift in Indian foreign policy, permanently altering the subcontinent’s security architecture.

The roots of this stalemate can be found in the structural failures of past diplomacy. In 1947, 1965, and 1971, Pakistan initiated conventional wars, none of which delivered the results it desired. The third resulted in the breakup of the country and the birth of independent Bangladesh.

These experiences, together with the success of the US-backed mujahideen in their fight against Soviet forces in Afghanistan in the late 1980s, prompted Pakistan’s military to embrace a new strategy, based on asymmetrical warfare—or, more bluntly, terrorism.
From 1989 to 1993, as terrorist attacks caused significant civilian casualties in India, Pakistani officers crowed about “bleeding India to death by a thousand cuts”.
Indian leaders were nonetheless convinced that structured dialogue could persuade Pakistan to abandon this strategy. This belief gave rise to the Composite Dialogue framework in the late 1990s.
This bureaucratic mechanism was designed to segment contentious issues—ranging from Kashmir to trade and humanitarian concerns—so that friction in one area would not derail progress in others.
There was just one problem: every major Indian peace overture was met with an act of military or terrorist provocation that the Pakistani government was either unable or unwilling to prevent.

In 1999, when then-Indian prime minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee undertook his historic bus journey to Lahore to sign a landmark peace declaration, Pakistani troops were infiltrating the Kargil district of Ladakh—actions that led to the Kargil War (which Pakistan lost).

In 2008, when back-channel diplomacy was on the brink of delivering a non-territorial solution to the Kashmir issue, coordinated terrorist attacks by Pakistan-based militants killed 166 innocent civilians in Mumbai.

This cycle exposed a profound institutional disconnect within Pakistan. Its civilian governments lacked the authority or longevity to fulfill the commitments they made at the negotiating table, and its military-intelligence apparatus viewed peace with India as an existential threat to its domestic hegemony.

Now, India has had enough. Prime Minister Narendra Modi initially followed the old peacemaking script. He invited his Pakistani counterpart, Nawaz Sharif, to his 2014 inauguration, and visited Lahore the following year.
Even when this visit was followed by a terrorist attack on the Indian airbase in Pathankot, Modi invited Sharif to join the official investigation into the incident.
Then came the final straw: Pakistan’s joint investigation team concluded that the attack was a “drama staged by India to malign Pakistan”.

With that, India abandoned its doctrine of strategic restraint in favour of a new guiding dictum: talks and terror cannot coexist. India would return to the negotiating table only after Pakistan dismantled, comprehensively and verifiably, its state-supported terrorist networks.

This diplomatic shift was accompanied by a fundamental change in India’s military doctrine. For nearly three decades, Pakistan assumed that its tactical nuclear arsenal would deter India from launching conventional military reprisals for terrorist attacks. Then India decided to call Pakistan’s bluff—most notably, in last year’s “Operation Sindoor”.

Through calibrated retaliatory actions, ranging from surgical cross-border strikes to sophisticated aerial bombardments targeting terrorist infrastructure deep within Pakistani territory, India demonstrated a willingness to accept escalation risks to impose tangible costs on its neighbour.
By signalling that state-sponsored terror would automatically trigger a conventional military response, India has sought to rewrite the rules of deterrence in South Asia.
The current stalemate is hardly desirable. The absence of a diplomatic safety valve between nuclear-armed neighbours poses acute risks to regional, even global, stability.

Even the most basic bilateral matters, such as humanitarian issues, trade blockades, and water sharing, are now viewed through a hyper-politicised national-security lens. And if a new crisis erupts, what mechanism is available to manage it? The margin for miscalculation is perilously thin.

But the prospects for a diplomatic breakthrough remain bleak. Pakistan’s military leadership still pins its domestic political legitimacy partly on hostility towards India, even as the country faces profound economic distress. And India, with its growing economic and conventional-military advantages, has little reason to compromise on its core security interests.

The US is certainly not encouraging India to rethink this stance. Not only has Donald Trump’s administration all but abandoned America’s Indo-Pacific strategy, in which India played a central role as a critical counterweight to a rising China, it has also embraced Pakistan, which, despite its financial instability and close ties with China, has managed to woo the US administration by striking a lucrative cryptocurrency deal with a Trump-linked firm and unctuously nominating Trump for a Nobel Peace Prize.

With the underpinnings of the India-Pakistan conflict firmly entrenched, the current stalemate should be viewed not as a pause between rounds of negotiation, but rather as part of a deliberate strategy of disengagement.

Until Pakistan undergoes a political transformation that fundamentally alters its security calculus, or a “black swan” event forces an existential realignment of regional priorities, the silence across the subcontinent will endure—and the risk of catastrophic error will remain.

Shashi Tharoor, a former UN under-secretary-general and former Indian minister of state for external affairs and human resource development, is a fourth-term elected MP for the opposition Indian National Congress.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

a862bb5fa635cfe9: Microsoft took down the Exchange Admin Center (EAC) today after a code change left administrators facing an "Internal Server Error" when trying to access the service. Microsoft first admitted that something was amiss at 0937 UTC on October 12, noting, "When attempting to access the Exchange admin center, affected admins may encounter an 'Internal Server Error' message." Any administrator attempting to access the EAC could be affected. It was more than an hour before the company stated: "We've identified unexpected 302 redirect errors during affected Exchange admin center (EAC) access attempts and are analyzing diagnostic logs to isolate the source of the access failures. "While we continue our investigation, admins remain unable to access the EAC, with no workaround currently available." So, a fun morning for Microsoft's European users. According to Microsoft, the EAC is "a modern, web-based management console for managing Exchange Online." Want to manage mailboxes? EAC is where you go. Group management? Again, EAC. Microsoft explained: "The design of the EAC in Exchange Online aligns with the overall Microsoft 365 admin experience." Sadly, that alignment appears to extend to service wobbles caused by changes rolled out without due care and attention. Two hours after admitting things had gone awry, Microsoft said it was "continuing to test the rollback of the recent Exchange admin center (EAC) change while monitoring the results to determine if this resolves the impact." At this point, administrators were nodding sagely at an all-too familiar story. Of course rolling back the change did the trick. Microsoft stated as much in its final update: "A recent EAC configuration change resulted in unexpected HTTP responses within the affected request path, preventing admins from successfully accessing the EAC. "Reverting the identified change restored expected service functionality." Microsoft also assured customers it was reviewing the change to ensure it didn't make the same mistake again, as well as its monitoring and telemetry, to "improve detection and alerting for similar service behavior." The problem is that this is hardly a new phenomenon. In September, Microsoft made a configuration change that left some users unable to access SharePoint Online sites and pages. In April, another ill-thought-through change took down Outlook for iOS. And, in 2025, Microsoft 365 tumbled from the cloud because of yet another configuration change. It's almost as if testing changes consists of little more than asking Copilot, "does this look alright to you?" and then hitting the go button. The latest outage was resolved before the end of the working day, and a preliminary Post-Incident Report is due within two business days, with a final report due next week. Hopefully one or the other will contain words along the lines of "Hey, this keeps happening, maybe we should do some more testing before deploying to production?" ®

3f4c6d05dd16a54d: If you thought everyone was into chatbots, think again: about half of US adults never use the AI tools, and most have no interest in starting. According to Pew Research Center, older adults are the least likely to use chatbots, with roughly three-quarters of those aged 65 and older saying they never use them. That may be expected, yet more than half (58 percent) of adults aged 50 to 64 don't use them either. Those aged 18 to 29 use chatbots the most, at 66 percent, however even a third of them say they never do. About four in ten under 50 report not using them at all. Across all adults, 51 percent are chatbot refuseniks, so users are - just barely - the minority. Pew asked non-users to choose from five possible reasons. Six in ten cited simple lack of interest as a major factor, followed by the more familiar concerns of data privacy and the accuracy of chatbot answers. Some Reg readers might suspect older people avoid chatbots because they lack tech-savviness, but fewer than a third cited not knowing how to use them as a major reason. The authors of the survey also found fewer than one in five worried about what others might think of them for using the technology, so social stigma isn’t the deterrent either. Adoption also differs by race and ethnicity: non-users are more likely to be white, black or hispanic than Asian, according to Pew’s survey. The AI dodgers don't look ready to budge. Two-thirds (67 percent) say they’re unlikely to use the technology in the next 12 months, including 40 percent who say they’re not at all likely to change their mind. Another 12 percent are unsure, and just 5 percent of non-users think they'll probably try a chatbot over the next year. Perhaps abstainers were put off by a bad experience, such as Microsoft’s notorious racist chatbot Tay a decade ago. Or something more recent, like the Trump administration’s official America.gov service, which at the time of writing still displays a hotdog if you type that into the prompt. ®

f046a994d6828ccc: What is DNS? That's right, it's a database. You can disagree with me but you would be wrong. What can you put in a database? Strings, ints (and you learn the difference right quick if your AWS account ID has a leading zero!), JSON objects, coordinates; some of the databases out there have some pretty esoteric types. PostgreSQL supports circle, a polygon, a macaddr8, and a tsquery. Oracle will store a ROWID and your dignity. In a word, databases store data. Can you put answers in a database? Well sure; you could record that "3 + 2 is equal to 5" and store that answer. You can do the same with comparison operators; "3 is larger than 2" and so on. Take it a step further and you've built something with your database: a remarkably inconvenient calculator. So now we've established that you can store arithmetic and decisions in a database. And what can we do with those things? That's right, we can follow instructions! Good job! And what does following instructions require? Generally, memory; a place to store your numbers, your instructions, and which instruction comes next. If only we had a place to store those things. Oh right, we do; we have a database! Now connect those lookups together. Read an instruction, look up an answer, save the result, repeat as needed. So what have we built? That's right: a computer! And what can a computer run? Programs! My, you're quite good at this. And now, gentle reader: what program do we apparently have a moral obligation to run on every computer? Oh yes, though many of you are going to sit back and instead say "oh no" as the horror courses through you. I am talking about Doom. This very publication agrees with me! What have I done? That's right; I have compiled Doom for a 32-bit machine whose arithmetic and memory live in DNS. A small program supplies the wiring and the clock, neither of which the architects of DNS saw fit to include. But DNS does supply the answers. So, can we play Doom? Only if it's turn-based. It won't render on human timescales anyway. In my first attempt, I pressed Right, and then waited for 577 seconds to find out what happened. By using native transport, pipelining, packing registers densely, and optimizing instruction blocks, I was able to drop that to 146 seconds, before I hit a wall. BIND answers in about 7 µs per query over TCP and 4 µs over UDP, which is fast. The problem is that a 32-bit add is four DNS lookups, a branch is five, and a frame needs 6.6 million of them, so don't use a server that charges per request. And what do we do when BIND isn't performing the way we want it to? I don't know what you do, but I publish my code, then reach out to Paul Vixie, DNS pioneer and architect of BIND 8 to unjustifiably complain. Paul then apparently congratulates me on "the best use of RFC 2136 DNS UPDATE" that he'd ever seen. Given that he's a co-author of that RFC, I suspect he's seen a lot! Which was gratifying, but unhelpful. So let's take another crack at it. What if I do lookaheads? Good thought, bad outcome, because BIND is bound by message count, not chain depth. Well okay, I have some more tricks in my Big Bag of Stupid Ideas. So I went a bit further and via committing registers to DNS less often, moving lookups to UDP, telling BIND to stop padding answers with authority records, and requiring fewer lookups per instruction, I was ultimately able to get that press-right time down from 577 seconds to 146.3 seconds to 54.4 seconds, for a 10.6x improvement. And now I think I have hit a wall. Even at one DNS exchange per instruction (which is far better than anything realistically achievable), 1.4 million instructions at roughly 10 µs each is 14 seconds per tick. Doom says its tic rate is 35 per second, so "playable" is a tic every 28.6 ms. I remain at 54,000 ms, which is three orders of magnitude away from victory. Okay seriously, WHAT? This legitimately works. Every commit is an RFC 2136 UPDATE with a hard requirement: it fails unless the previous state is still exactly what was last written. Apparently "real" database people call that optimistic concurrency, or compare-and-swap. Joke's on you, friends; DNS has shipped with that since 1997; has your inferior database? The database itself is 6.4 million rows of truth tables. ff.01.0.add holds "001": 255 plus 1 is 00 carry 1. DNS is just acting as a librarian here, fetching memorized answers to any arithmetic question in-scope and returning the answer upon request. It's also verifiable! The frame that's spat out is checked on every pixel against an independent emulator. If one record is corrupted in the AND table, the answer changes, which proves there's no local fallback doing arithmetic for us. I've included tooling so that reviewers can run two commands against that repo and verify correctness. I also confess I cheated slightly here; the run I'm pulling these numbers from started from a checkpoint prepared by a normal emulator. It turns out that for SOME UNKNOWN REASON getting a cold boot through Doom's startup screens via DNS would take hours. Also, before the timer starts, DNS has to load those 6.4 million records, so it's a computer that takes roughly a minute to boot before it can even start. We can't cheat This runs atop nothing special: Debian's stock BIND 9.20, configured through named.conf. It lives in a container with networking disabled. I want to be very clear here: this isn't DNS pretending to be a CPU. The instruction decoding is done ahead of time by a compiler; BIND never executes an instruction itself. All that it sees is a key-value read, a conditional write, and 6.4 million rows of precomputed answers. So instead, think of this monstrosity as a database with a key-value read, a conditional write, and 6.4 million rows of precomputed answers. It's not really a computer; it's simply a very good database. And that turns out to be enough. ®

273a91b33201d9e7: UCLA and Oracle have settled a dispute over a troubled ERP project originally budgeted at $120 million, with the vendor waiving $1.31 million in outstanding fees and granting $3.1 million in credits against future charges. In May, the University of California's Compliance and Audit Committee recommended a settlement [PDF] of UCLA's pre-litigation dispute with Oracle, which the Board of Regents approved. According to documents released in response to a California Public Records Act request, UCLA stopped paying its Oracle subscription in September 2024 over what it described as shortcomings in grants management functionality. UCLA and Oracle signed their first agreement relating to the project – called Ascend – in November 2017. The project had a revised go-live date of January 2025, but was paused in mid-2024. The settlement records UCLA's allegation that "the ERP Cloud Services did not perform as warranted in the Oracle Agreement." "The ERP Cloud Services lacked sufficient functionality to meet the University's requirements and could not be used by the University as expected," said the document, which was seen by The Register. It continued that "the University incurred costs and delays due to the ERP Cloud Services inability to meet the University's requirements." It added: "As a result, Oracle breached the Oracle Agreement." Under the settlement, UCLA agreed to pay Oracle $350,000 of the $1.66 million in outstanding invoices. Oracle then waived the remaining balance – $1.31 million – and credited $3.1 million against future Oracle fees. These credits expire at the end of May 2028. The agreement says the university should not make public statements about its terms, which are to remain confidential, although both parties acknowledged that UCLA is subject to the California Public Records Act. The Register has asked Oracle to comment. The settlement was obtained by California resident Eric Guyer, founder of independent Oracle cost consultancy Advizant. In a social media post, he said that the credits suggested UCLA would continue with the project in some form, with Oracle as the main vendor. Guyer suggested Oracle most likely discounted its software to win the "coveted" UCLA logo. He estimated the total subscription value at around $12 million over ten years. He said Oracle tends to move decisively when unpaid bills on clear contractual terms back it into a corner. "This is rare despite the lore of its litigious nature. Everyone has a line. In any case, UCLA's claim probably went to Oracle because it was the easiest to point a finger at: consultants sell effort, not outcomes, and internal staff can only be fired." However, he said the average customer should not conclude that claiming a breach and stopping payment is advisable. "It can be effective, but is an exceedingly painful path," he claimed. "In this rare case, Oracle agreed to eat some shit at the end of a poorly planned implementation in exchange for UCLA's silence in the fiercely competitive higher ed market. In other public implementation fights, Oracle struck first or countersued, with press releases to match." UCLA serves around 49,000 students and manages a budget of around $11 billion. A 2025 report [PDF] presented to the University of California Board of Regents' Finance and Capital Strategies Committee said that among the "Top Issues, Risks and Challenges" the UCLA project leadership faced was "Oracle's lack of responsiveness – particularly regarding licensing costs and support." It added that the project's original $120 million budget was revised down to $98.9 million, with $13.5 million remaining as of December 31, 2024. The report, covering the period through December 2024, said the project started in April 2018 and was originally expected to end in July 2020. The document described it as a "comprehensive business transformation initiative" to modernize the university's financial, budgetary, and research administration operations by moving to Oracle Cloud SaaS. It also included retrofitting any systems that connected with the main finance system. The procurement module, BruinBuy Plus, went live in January 2024, but the main "Oracle Financials go-live has been paused since August 2 [2024] and is undergoing program assessment," the document said. Among the mitigation plans in the review was to "finalize the decision on whether to continue with the current vendor or explore alternatives" based on a reassessment of the tool and provider. According to the settlement document, the University told Oracle via email on June 20, 2025 that the "University wanted to terminate the Ascend project and the ERP Cloud Services." In May, a spokesperson for UCLA said in a statement to The Register: "The University continues to evaluate the most effective path forward for financial systems modernization." Under the terms of the settlement agreement, the University and Oracle have agreed to make no further claims for damages related to the contract dispute, and neither has admitted liability. According to a report from campus newspaper Daily Bruin, UCLA was still using legacy financial systems software designed in the 1980s when the budget was just seven percent of its current size. 3a228466c214dfd8: London's minicab drivers want Mayor Sadiq Khan to put the brakes on robotaxis before they threaten thousands of jobs, with a new City Hall report casting doubt on whether the capital is ready for driverless cars. The Independent Workers' Union of Great Britain (IWGB) has called on Transport for London (TfL) to halt the rollout following the publication of a London Assembly Transport Committee report on Monday. The 66-page report makes uncomfortable reading for the companies hoping to unleash fleets of driverless taxis on London's streets. "As it stands, we currently have not heard sufficient evidence to persuade us that London should welcome autonomous passenger services," it concludes. Google's Waymo, British startup Wayve, and Chinese tech giant Baidu are among those gearing up to bring autonomous passenger services to London. Waymo has already been testing its cars in the capital and hopes to launch a commercial fleet of "low hundreds" this year, subject to regulatory approval. Uber and Wayve have secured TfL private hire licenses for vehicles offering supervised self-driving rides, meaning a human driver remains legally in control, and Freenow and Baidu are targeting a fully driverless launch in 2027. London has around 105,000 licensed private hire drivers, many of whom have reason to worry about cars that can do their jobs without them. "Every car feeds a family, and the prospect of not being able to earn money leaves us all with a deep uncertainty as to how we will provide for them. We already struggle to get by as it is," said Gholomreza "Rez" Kamyabi, an Uber driver and vice chair of the IWGB Private Hire Drivers union. The committee heard warnings that robotaxis could put large numbers of drivers out of work, and wants TfL to work with unions and operators to retrain, redeploy, and fund those affected. The IWGB, however, wants the rollout stopped. "The IWGB Private Hire Drivers Union opposes the rollout of driverless cars," said union president Alex Marshall, warning the technology could put thousands out of work while benefiting tech companies and investors. Jobs aren't the only concern. Under the government's interim Automated Passenger Services permitting scheme, the Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency (DVSA) issues operating permits. TfL must consent before a service launches in London, but cannot independently suspend or revoke a permit once issued. TfL also has no formal say over existing driverless trials, and operators aren't legally required to report incidents to it, although some have shared information voluntarily. The report details several incidents involving autonomous test vehicles, including a car reportedly entering a police crime scene cordon in April, another filmed turning the wrong way into a one-way street in June, and a reported collision with a motorcycle in July. It also questions how robotaxis would handle medical emergencies, passenger safety, and accessibility. None of the autonomous vehicles currently being trialed are wheelchair accessible. Then there's congestion. Robotaxis could lure passengers away from public transportation while adding more traffic as vehicles travel empty between fares. The committee wants operators to report their empty mileage so TfL can assess the impact. Londoners aren't exactly clamoring for the technology either. A YouGov survey commissioned by the committee found that 42 percent opposed autonomous passenger vehicles, compared with 29 percent who supported them. Just 29 percent said they would be likely to use one. The committee stopped short of calling for a ban, instead recommending tougher safety requirements, giving TfL powers to cap vehicle numbers, and a process to request the immediate suspension of permits. It also wants TfL to take over permitting when the Automated Vehicles Act is fully implemented, expected in the second half of 2027. At the time of the investigation, TfL had not yet published the criteria it would use to approve driverless passenger services. So London is preparing for robotaxis while its transport authority works out the rules, Assembly members question the benefits, and cab drivers demand the whole thing be stopped. Still, at least the cars won't complain about their working conditions.®

4716b75a3ed74c46: A piece of internet history that once traveled strapped to a pigeon's leg is up for auction at Christie's, where someone has already bid $4,000 for what might be the world's most expensive ping. The unusual lot is a surviving IP packet from a 2001 experiment in which Norwegian Linux enthusiasts decided to find out whether the internet could, in fact, run on birds. The idea dates back to April 1, 1990, when American network engineer David Waitzman published RFC 1149, titled A Standard for the Transmission of IP Datagrams on Avian Carriers. Written in the wonderfully dry language of an official internet standards document, the April Fools' proposal outlined how carrier pigeons could transport IP datagrams between locations. It noted that avian carriers could provide high bandwidth, although latency would be another matter entirely. Most people appreciated the joke and moved on. The Bergen Linux User Group (BLUG), however, decided to actually build the thing. On April 28, 2001, the group put RFC 1149 to the test using racing pigeons, printers, and scanners. IP packets were printed as hexadecimal strings on strips of paper, attached to the birds' legs, and flown between two lofts 5km (roughly 3 miles) apart. The results hardly amounted to a ringing endorsement of pigeon-powered networking. Nine packets were dispatched, but only four replies came back, giving the experiment a packet-loss rate of about 56 percent. Still, the network worked, at least in the loosest possible sense of the word. Actual IP packets had traveled through the air without a single router, fiber-optic cable, or telecoms provider getting involved. One of those packets has now resurfaced at auction house Christie's as part of its Fine Printed Books & Manuscripts Including Americana and Science auction. The item is a small scroll of paper measuring just 41mm by 210mm, complete with creases from being rolled up and attached to the pigeon's leg. It is now framed, with an inscription on the reverse identifying it as the property of Waitzman, to whom it was presented in 2002. Christie's initially estimated the packet would fetch between $2,000 and $3,000, but bidding has already reached $4,000. The auction closes on October 13. The auction house describes the experiment as an example of the internet's tradition of the "artful hack," celebrating the technical ingenuity and sense of humor of its early community. There is, of course, something rather fitting about an internet packet that took to the skies 25 years ago now commanding thousands of dollars. Most packets disappear into the ether once they've served their purpose. This one ended up in a frame and is being sold by Christie's. Not bad for something delivered by a pigeon. ®
